newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government asks Di Pietro to reconsider.
newsitem.headline: Italian government asks Di Pietro to reconsider.

text.p: Cabinet ministers are pleading with Italy's most popular public figure, Antonio Di Pietro, not to resign as public works minister. But the impulsive former star magistrate showed no sign on Saturday of changing his mind.

The government issued a statement after a cabinet meeting on Saturday saying Di Pietro's resignation had been rejected and that Prime Minister Romano Prodi would make a fresh attempt to persuade him to stay.
"Prime Minister Prodi intends to make every possible effort to get him to him reconsider his decision," said Cabinet Secretary Enrico Micheli, adding that the two men would meet soon.
But Di Pietro, by far the most respected figure in Italy's public life, appeared to be in no mood to return to government. Newspapers said he was incomunicado and his whereabouts unknown.

Di Pietro stormed out of the government on Thursday after coming under investigation for alleged malpractice during his time in a team of graft-busting Milan magistrates that broke the back of Italy's old political guard in the early 1990s.

The resignation, which Di Pietro said was irrevocable, was deeply unsettling for the government, which is trying to railroad a tough 1997 budget package through parliament in the teeth of bitter opposition.
Political friends and foes said Di Pietro's nerves appeared to have snapped at the prospect of a fresh investigation.
But if he clears his name he is widely expected to make a swift return to politics and commentators believe he could find the temptation to create his own political party irresistible.

Di Pietro was the target of an earlier probe into allegations of corruption and of profiting from holding a public office. All charges against him were dropped in April shortly before Prodi named him to his cabinet.

Di Pietro has portrayed the investigations against him as a vendetta by players in the scandal he exposed who want to cast doubt on the integrity of the celebrated "Tangentopoli" -- Bribesville -- probes that brought down the old political order.
Massimo d'Alema, leader of the left-wing Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) which forms the backbone of Prodi's coalition, said he had spoken to Di Pietro and found him deeply unnerved.
"At the other end of the telephone line I sensed a man who was really upset, very shaken," D'Alema told Rome's La Repubblica newspaper.
Umberto Bossi, the firebrand leader of the secessionist Northern League, was less sympathetic, saying Di Pietro did not have the temperament to handle the rough and tumble of politics.
"He is a little upstart whose nerves go to pieces a bit too easily," said Bossi.
But Bossi suggested Di Pietro's dramatic exit from the government may have been more calculated than it appeared.
"He probably realised that by staying in a government which is losing consensus every day he would have muddied the image of himself that he has built up," added Bossi.

An opinion poll showed Di Pietro's popularity had soared since his departure. The poll, conducted by Directa on Friday, said his approval rating rose to 89 percent from 75.4 percent in an earlier poll and that 72.4 percent of those polled wanted him to found his own political party.
"The impact of Di Pietro on the collective imagination is very strong. People see him as a hero fighting a conspiracy and they end up identifying with him," said Directa's President Giorgio Calo.
